title: An Experimental Survey Tool for Measuring the Five Key Beliefs
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. shares a practical 20-question Likert-scale survey tool he has developed and used to measure students' Five Key Beliefs in his own classroom, reporting that it has given him reliable and actionable insights each time he has deployed it. He explains his setup protocol — emphasizing student honesty and the collection of individual-level data via email — so that specific students can be identified and targeted for intervention rather than just tracking class-level averages. Each survey question is annotated with its belief dimension (CR, VAL, EFF, BEL), providing immediate diagnostic information pointing toward the relevant strategies in The Will to Learn. Stuart Jr. describes a two-pronged interpretation process: first, identifying students with scores of 1 or 2 as signals of acute struggle warranting immediate intervention; second, using class-level patterns — such as uniformly low Value scores — to guide classroom-level strategy selection. Two open-ended items about meaning and personal growth round out the instrument, providing qualitative richness alongside the Likert data.
points: Collect individual student emails in the survey to identify specific students who score 1 or 2 on any belief dimension — low scores are signals of acute struggle, not just low averages.

Code each question to its belief dimension so that low scores provide immediate diagnostic information pointing to specific strategies: CR items to MGCs, VAL items to mini-sermons, EFF items to outcome-unpacking, BEL items to belonging strategies.
Students with low Credibility scores on connection-related items (e.g., Q6 on individual check-ins) can often be addressed immediately with a single focused MGC in the next class period.
Class-wide low scores on Value questions call for classroom-level strategies like Mini-Sermons or Valued Within exercises, shifting the intervention from individual to structural.

The two open-ended questions — about what has helped students believe school matters and what they no longer struggle with — provide qualitative depth that complements the Likert data and reveals the logic behind the numbers.
quotes: Though I'm surely not a survey-specialist-guy, I've developed a survey tool for measuring the Five Key Beliefs that I wanted to share today. It has given me reliable, actionable insights both times I've used it (Spring and Fall of 2025), so I'd like to give it to you in case it helps.

As your teacher, I am very interested in your honest experiences and feelings toward the work of learning we do in this class. I'm not sharing this with anyone else. Just be honest and don't overthink the questions. I'll give you about 10 minutes to do some thoughtful work here.

The reason I collect student emails is that I want to be able to see this data for individual students. For me, the power of this tool is less about getting a general impression of the level of the Five Key Beliefs in the overall classroom and more about getting specific insights into specific students.

First, look for students with low numbers — 1 or 2 — in any of the questions. These, to me, are cries for help. When a student clicks 1 or 2, they're saying, "This is an area where I'm having a hard time.

What I love most about this survey is that I can find cases in which immediate intervention (e.g., an MGC, checking in on the students' concerns about success, identifying kids who feel strongly that they don't belong) might help a lot and rather quickly.
